Chapter 3: The Weight of Poverty and Rural Life
Living in poverty—it’s so much more than just not having enough money. It’s the daily mental math, the small moments of embarrassment, and the way it quietly shapes every decision you make. Out in rural Oregon, the scenery is breathtaking, but life there can be downright unforgiving.
Jobs are few and far between. Opportunities? They feel a world away. For so many families, getting by means learning how to make less go further, finding creative ways to stretch every single dollar.
Picture a child growing up here. Pretty soon, you learn not to ask for new clothes or toys—it just isn’t in the cards. But there’s a kind of quiet pride that comes from making things last: patching up an old pair of jeans, reusing last year’s notebooks, turning leftovers into a whole new meal. The local thrift shop turns into a gold mine, and when a neighbor drops off a bag of hand-me-downs—even if the fit’s a little off—you’re grateful.
School isn’t always a refuge. Field trips and clubs sound fun until you see the price tag. There’s always this awareness—you don’t have the latest shoes, or the newest phone. Some teachers notice, offering gentle support. Others seem to miss it entirely. And that feeling of shame? It’s never really spoken, but you carry it with you every day.
In a small town, everyone knows everyone’s story. The community is close, but it can be cautious, too. Word spreads fast, and sometimes, it feels like everyone’s watching. There’s solidarity among those who are struggling, but also a real fear of being judged. Some families do their best to hide their hardships, hoping no one will notice. Others? They wear their struggles openly, refusing to feel ashamed for things they can’t control.
Work isn’t just for the adults. Kids pitch in, helping with chores, picking up odd jobs for a little extra cash. That sense of responsibility comes early—watching younger siblings, fixing things around the house, learning to cook and clean. Sure, it’s born out of necessity, but it also brings a sense of competence and pride.
Nature is always there—a comfort and a challenge. The woods and fields offer a space to play, or just to get away when things at home get tense. But rural life also means isolation. It’s a long drive to school, to the store, to anything fun. You feel the lack of resources everywhere—from healthcare, to education, even just simple ways to relax.
Most people don’t realize how much creativity it takes just to get by. Fixing a broken appliance with whatever parts you can find. Growing vegetables in a tiny backyard patch. Swapping goods or favors with neighbors. Over time, these acts of resourcefulness become second nature. It’s exhausting, but there’s something empowering about it, too.
And then there’s the stigma—that heavy, invisible weight. The pressure to keep up appearances, to make it seem like things are better than they really are. But here’s something important: being honest about the struggle can actually set you free. Admitting what you’re going through? That’s the first step toward making things better.
